item.title: Australia’s trade surplus jumps to A$2.8 billion, a seven-month high, on LNG and metals
item.description:
A stronger trade surplus is modestly supportive for the Australian dollar, reinforcing the currency’s link to commodity prices. With energy prices elevated by the Middle East conflict, Australia is better placed than many importers, as LNG and coal export earnings help cushion a rising fuel bill. The data are unlikely to shift Reserve Bank of Australia expectations on their own, given the volatile gold component. Traders will look to upcoming volume data for a cleaner read on how much net exports are adding to growth.

--

Gas and metals did the heavy lifting for Australia’s trade surplus in September, with a big drop in gold imports doing the rest.

Summary:

  • Australia’s goods trade surplus widened to about A$2.8 billion in September, the largest in seven months
  • That was up from A$184 million in August and well above forecasts
  • Exports rose 2.3% from the month before, led by other mineral fuels, including LNG, and metals
  • Imports fell 3.3%, driven by a nearly 35% drop in gold imports
  • Higher fuel prices have yet to show up meaningfully in the import bill

Australia’s goods trade surplus widened sharply in September to its largest in seven months, as a rise in exports of liquefied natural gas and metals coincided with a steep fall in gold imports, data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics showed on Thursday.

The surplus on goods trade came in at about A$2.8 billion (around US$2 billion), up from A$184 million in August and well ahead of forecasts for a surplus of roughly A$1 billion or less.

Exports rose 2.3% from the previous month, following a 3.7% gain in August. The increase was driven by other mineral fuels, a category that includes liquefied natural gas, and by metals, highlighting the support Australia’s resource sector continues to draw from global commodity demand.

Imports fell 3.3%, reversing a 5.8% rise in August. The decline was led by gold, where imports dropped by nearly 35%. Gold flows can be volatile from month to month and often swing the headline balance, so the scale of the drop flatters the underlying improvement to some degree.

The figures also suggest the recent rebound in fuel prices has yet to show up meaningfully in the import bill. As a large importer of refined fuel, Australia’s import costs would be expected to rise if higher prices persist, which could narrow the surplus in coming months.

At the same time, higher energy prices tend to cut both ways for Australia. As a major exporter of liquefied natural gas and coal, the country benefits from elevated global energy prices on the export side, partly offsetting the cost of more expensive fuel imports.

The stronger trade position is a positive for the economy’s external accounts, though its contribution to growth will depend on how the volume of trade, rather than its value, develops over the quarter.

Attention now turns to whether commodity export strength can be sustained, and how quickly rising fuel costs feed into imports. Both will shape whether September proves a high point for the surplus or the start of a firmer trend. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Japan services PMI edges up to 51.7, but composite slips to five-month low as hiring slows
item.description:
The data offer something for both sides of the BoJ debate: historically sharp cost pressures support further tightening, while slowing hiring and weaker confidence give the cautious camp ammunition. On balance, the release is unlikely to shift December pricing materially, leaving the yen more sensitive to the BoJ minutes and oil-driven inflation signals. Firms citing inflation as a drag on confidence underlines how energy costs from the Middle East are feeding into Japanese business sentiment. Weak export orders point to limited support from overseas demand.

--

Earlier:

  • BoJ minutes: board backed further hikes, flagged 50% oil surge as government urged caution

--

Japan’s service providers are still growing and still paying up, but they’re hiring less and feeling gloomier about it.

Summary:

  • The services PMI rose to 51.7 in October from 51.3, a fifth month of expansion, driven by domestic demand
  • The composite PMI slipped to 52.1 from 52.3, a five-month low, as manufacturing growth slowed
  • Services hiring rose at the slowest pace in 14 months; across the private sector, job creation hit a one-year low
  • Input cost inflation eased to an eight-month low but stayed well above its long-run average
  • Services confidence fell to its weakest since March, citing inflation, ageing and labour shortages
  • S&P Global said growth momentum and cost pressures will be key for BoJ tightening decisions

Japan’s services sector grew at a slightly faster pace in October, but a slowdown in manufacturing pulled overall private sector growth to a five-month low, while still-sharp cost pressures kept inflation in focus for the Bank of Japan, according to S&P Global’s latest survey.

The S&P Global Japan Services PMI rose to 51.7 in October from 51.3 in September, marking a fifth straight month of expansion. Firms said stronger inflows of new work and efforts to broaden their customer base lifted activity, though growth remained modest and below the average so far this year.

New orders also picked up slightly, driven by firmer domestic demand. Export business fell again, although the decline was the smallest in six months.

Hiring was the weak spot. Services employment rose only marginally, the slowest pace in the current 14-month run of job creation, as some firms reported staff leaving through resignations and retirements. With capacity stretched, backlogs of work increased again.

Price pressures slowed but stayed elevated. Input cost inflation fell to an eight-month low and output charges also rose more slowly, yet both remained well above their long-run averages. Business confidence about the year ahead dropped to its weakest since March, with firms citing inflation, an ageing population and labour shortages.

The broader picture was softer. The composite PMI, which combines services and manufacturing, slipped to 52.1 from 52.3, its lowest since May, though it still pointed to a 19th consecutive month of growth. Faster services growth was offset by a slower rise in factory output. Across the private sector, job creation slowed to a one-year low and confidence fell to a three-month low. Input costs rose at a historically sharp rate, while growth in prices charged eased to a four-month low.

S&P Global said input costs and selling prices, while rising more slowly, were still increasing at a pace that suggests official consumer inflation could stay elevated in the coming months. It added that whether growth loses further momentum and whether cost pressures ease will be key considerations for the BoJ as it weighs further tightening, warning that persistent inflation weighed on confidence and could also constrain demand and hiring.

The data arrive on the same day as minutes from the BoJ’s September meeting, which showed policymakers agreed on the need for further rate increases, keeping attention on whether the central bank moves again in December. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6783 – Reuters estimate
item.description:
Earlier this week:

  • China’s PBOC lifts FX reserve ratio to 6%: what it means for the yuan, AUD

-

The People’s Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day’s closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point. A stronger-than-expected CNY midpoint is typically read as a sign the PBOC is leaning against depreciation pressure, while a weaker fixing for the CNY can indicate tolerance for a softer currency, often in response to dollar strength or domestic economic headwinds.In periods of heightened global volatility, such as shifts in US rate expectations, trade tensions or capital flow pressures, the fixing takes on added significance. For investors, it provides insight into Beijing’s currency priorities, balancing competitiveness, capital stability and financial market confidence.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: BoJ minutes: board backed further hikes, flagged 50% oil surge as government urged caution
item.description:
The minutes add a hawkish edge to the yen outlook, with talk of a faster pace and getting closer to neutral “relatively soon” supporting pricing for a December move. Against that, one member’s view that market expectations are running ahead of the economy may cap how far rate pricing extends, particularly at the longer end of the JGB curve. Oil is now an explicit driver of BoJ thinking, so renewed crude strength from the Middle East is likely to feed directly into Japanese rate expectations. The Cabinet Office’s call for caution is a reminder that political resistance to rapid tightening remains a factor.

-

The BoJ board in September was arguing over how fast to go, not whether to keep going, with oil doing much of the persuading.

Summary:

  • Members agreed the BoJ should keep raising rates as underlying inflation approached 2% and financial conditions stayed accommodative
  • Several saw a shift in policy phase, from lifting inflation to stabilising it around 2%; one said hikes may need to speed up if prices overshoot
  • One member said hasty action was unnecessary; dissenters Asada and Sato preferred holding at 1%
  • Crude was up about 50% since July, and a few members flagged the tail risk of physical oil shortages
  • The Cabinet Office urged careful examination of the cumulative effects of past hikes
  • The BoJ has since held at 1.25% in October, saying underlying inflation reached levels consistent with its target

Bank of Japan policymakers agreed at their September meeting that the central bank should keep raising interest rates, with some members arguing for a faster pace if prices threaten to overshoot, according to minutes released on Thursday that also showed the government urging caution over the cumulative effect of past hikes.

At the September 17 and 18 meeting, the BoJ raised its policy rate by 25 basis points to 1.25%, the highest since 1995, in a 7-2 vote. The minutes show members agreed it was appropriate to keep lifting rates and adjusting the degree of monetary accommodation, given that underlying inflation was approaching 2% and financial conditions remained accommodative.

Several members pointed to a shift in the phase of policy. One said the aim was no longer to push underlying inflation higher but to stabilise it around 2%. Another said the BoJ should show markets its determination to prevent prices overshooting by responding nimbly to overseas conditions. A third said the bank would need to speed up its rate hikes if signs of an upward deviation in prices emerged, while another favoured bringing rates closer to the neutral level relatively soon to leave room to move in either direction.

Not all were in a hurry. One member said underlying inflation was not accelerating fast enough to risk the bank falling behind the curve, so hasty action was unnecessary. The two dissenters, Toichiro Asada and Ayano Sato, preferred to hold at 1%. Asada argued that with core inflation below 2%, the economy could not necessarily be called strong, while Sato said economic and price trends had not substantially accelerated.

Oil featured heavily. One member noted crude prices had risen about 50% since July while the yen had appreciated about 5%, which would push up consumer prices considerably if sustained. A few members flagged the tail risk of physical shortages of crude, not just higher prices, citing the suspension of Saudi Arabia’s pipeline operations, unstable shipping through the Red Sea and falling reserves in the US and China.

Members also debated the neutral rate. One noted that a market gauge of the expected peak in rates had risen above 2%, while another said market expectations for hikes appeared somewhat ahead of the economy.

The government’s representatives struck a more cautious tone. The Cabinet Office said the BoJ should examine carefully the cumulative effects of past hikes, consider its neutral rate estimates and act appropriately in the event of excessive swings in the economy and markets.

Since the meeting, the BoJ held rates at 1.25% in October, while saying underlying inflation had reached levels consistent with its target. The minutes reinforce that the debate is over the pace of further tightening, not its direction, keeping attention on the December meeting.

Bank of Japan Governor Ueda 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: AstraZeneca makes $10 billion offer for obesity drugmaker Rhythm, WSJ reports
item.description:
The roughly 13% gap between Rhythm’s close and the reported offer price leaves room for a further move if talks are confirmed, but also reflects the risk that no deal materialises. The report is likely to lift interest in other mid-sized obesity and rare disease biotechs as potential targets, given the appetite large drugmakers are showing for the space. For AstraZeneca, a deal of this size is unlikely to move its shares materially but would signal it is willing to buy growth to hit its 2030 target. Chinese drug developers that have licensed obesity assets to Western groups may also draw attention as part of the same deal flow.

- AstraZeneca is reaching for a niche corner of the obesity boom, and paying a premium to get there.

Summary:

  • AstraZeneca made an offer of around $10 billion, or $124 a share, for Rhythm Pharmaceuticals last month, the WSJ reported, citing people familiar with the matter
  • Rhythm shares jumped 28% to just over $110, valuing the company at about $7.6 billion
  • Rhythm develops treatments for rare forms of obesity, including an approved drug for acquired hypothalamic obesity
  • A deal would add to AstraZeneca’s obesity pipeline and its rare disease business built on the Alexion acquisition
  • AstraZeneca targets $80 billion in sales by 2030, up from about $59 billion last year

AstraZeneca has made an offer of around $10 billion for Rhythm Pharmaceuticals, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing people familiar with the matter, in a move that would deepen the British drugmaker’s push into both obesity and rare disease treatments.

According to the report, AstraZeneca offered $124 a share for the US biotech last month, having previously expressed interest in the company. Rhythm’s shares were trading at around $95 on Wednesday afternoon before the report, implying a premium of roughly 30%. They closed up 28% at just over $110, valuing Rhythm at about $7.6 billion. The report did not include comment from either company, and the offer has not been confirmed.

The gap between Rhythm’s closing price and the reported offer, at roughly 13%, suggests investors see some uncertainty over whether a deal will be agreed on those terms.

Rhythm develops treatments for rare forms of obesity linked to the MC4R pathway, which regulates feelings of hunger. When the pathway malfunctions, it can trigger extreme, persistent hunger that leads to severe obesity. The company’s medicines include a treatment approved for acquired hypothalamic obesity, a rare condition.

The fit with AstraZeneca is twofold. The company has been building an obesity pipeline as it seeks a foothold in one of the fastest-growing areas of the drug market. It is developing several GLP-1 treatments, including one licensed from China’s Eccogene for about $185 million in 2023, and in January licensed a set of obesity and diabetes programmes from CSPC Pharmaceuticals, also based in China, for $1.2 billion upfront.

Rhythm would also add to AstraZeneca’s rare disease portfolio, which it built into a leading position through its $39 billion acquisition of Alexion in 2021.

The approach fits a broader strategy. AstraZeneca, valued at close to $300 billion and best known as a cancer drug powerhouse under Chief Executive Pascal Soriot, is targeting $80 billion in annual sales by 2030, up from about $59 billion last year. Analysts say deals will be needed to supplement its pipeline if it is to reach that goal.

A deal of around $10 billion would be modest relative to AstraZeneca’s size, but meaningful for a specialist obesity player, and would underline how large drugmakers are turning to acquisitions to secure growth. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Goldman Sachs: 45% of planned US data centre capacity faces state pauses, but likely short-lived
item.description:
The note gives investors a framework for Wednesday’s selloff in AI infrastructure stocks: a delay story rather than a demand collapse, which may limit further downside if pauses prove brief. A pull-forward of spending into 2027 could support near-term orders for chipmakers and power equipment suppliers, including Asian manufacturers tied to the buildout. Companies with power and permits already secured may gain relative value as new approvals slow. The main risk to the view is that pauses run longer than expected, which would shift the hit from timing to capacity.

---

Goldman sees the political backlash against data centres as a speed bump for the AI buildout, and possibly a reason to build faster before it arrives.

Summary:

  • Goldman estimates states likely to tighten data centre rules hold about 45% of planned US capacity
  • It expects temporary pauses in Texas, Georgia and Michigan while lawmakers weigh rules on power, water and tax breaks
  • Texas alone accounts for roughly a quarter of planned capacity
  • Goldman expects curbs to be short-lived, as data centres aren’t a top voter priority
  • Strategist Rich Privorotsky suggested some companies could pull spending into 2027 to beat new rules
  • The note follows a sharp fall in US AI infrastructure stocks on Wednesday

Goldman Sachs estimates that states likely to tighten rules on data centres account for about 45% of planned US capacity, flagging a new layer of risk for the AI infrastructure buildout after Democrats made gains in this week’s elections, though it expects any restrictions to prove temporary.

The bank’s economists expect Democrats in Texas, Georgia and Michigan to impose short-term pauses on new data centre projects while lawmakers consider tighter rules on electricity use, water consumption and tax incentives, according to reports of the note. Texas alone accounts for roughly a quarter of planned US capacity, making it the most significant of the three.

Goldman does not expect the curbs to last long, reasoning that data centres are not a top priority for voters and that political pressure is likely to ease once new frameworks are in place. That makes the risk one of timing rather than a lasting threat to capacity.

The timing effect may not run in the obvious direction. Goldman strategist Rich Privorotsky suggested some companies could bring spending forward into 2027 to get projects under way before new rules take effect, which could lift investment in the near term even as the medium-term pipeline faces delays.

The warning lands amid a sharp reassessment of the sector. US AI infrastructure stocks fell on Wednesday even as the broader market rallied, and other analysts have moved quickly to quantify the exposure, with one estimate putting more than 13 gigawatts of announced projects in Texas at risk. Several research houses have also cut price targets on companies that had been repositioning toward hosting AI workloads.

Goldman’s emphasis on state-level decisions echoes a view shared across much of this week’s research. UBS also highlighted state governments as more consequential for data centre projects than the change in control of Congress, even as it raised its AI capital spending forecasts.

The global significance lies in the supply chain. US data centre construction drives orders for chips, power equipment and cooling systems worldwide, so delays or a pull-forward in US projects would ripple through suppliers well beyond American borders. The key question now is how quickly states move, and whether pauses stay as short as Goldman expects. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: ICYMI: ADNOC denies report of third Hormuz bypass pipeline that could open to other producers
item.description:
A shared bypass line would chip away at the Hormuz risk premium over time by giving Gulf producers beyond the UAE a route to market that avoids the strait. With ADNOC’s denial, though, the report is unlikely to move crude near term, and the risk premium stays anchored to shipping attacks and transit volumes through the strait itself. The 2027 second line is the more tangible supply factor, potentially easing Asian buyers’ exposure to Hormuz disruption. Repeated attacks on Fujairah also limit how much comfort traders can take from bypass capacity, keeping the infrastructure itself part of the risk.

- The pipeline ADNOC says isn’t happening would have turned the UAE from a country avoiding Hormuz into one selling a way around it.

Summary:

  • Bloomberg reported ADNOC is weighing a third pipeline from the UAE’s west coast to Fujairah, bypassing Hormuz
  • The line could be open to third parties and was described to some Asian customers, but plans are not final
  • ADNOC called the report inaccurate and purely speculative
  • An existing line carries about 2 million barrels a day, and a second line due in 2027 would roughly double capacity
  • The UAE, Saudi Arabia and Kuwait are all pursuing ways to reduce reliance on the strait
  • Fujairah and Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline have both been attacked during the war

Abu Dhabi National Oil Co. has denied a report that it is weighing a third crude pipeline to bypass the Strait of Hormuz, a project that, according to Bloomberg, could be opened to other producers and turn the UAE’s east coast into a wider export outlet for Gulf oil.

Bloomberg reported on Wednesday, citing people familiar with the matter, that ADNOC was considering a new line from the UAE’s western coast to the port of Fujairah, which sits outside the strait on the Gulf of Oman. The pipeline could be made available to third parties, and ADNOC had described the plan to some Asian customers, the report said, adding that the project was not finalised and its route could change. No cost or timeline was given.

ADNOC told Bloomberg the report was inaccurate and purely speculative.

The third-party element is what sets the report apart from the UAE’s existing bypass strategy. ADNOC already operates a pipeline from its western onshore fields to Fujairah with capacity of about 2 million barrels a day, according to Bloomberg, and said in May it was accelerating a second line due for completion in 2027 that would roughly double that capacity. Both serve ADNOC’s own exports. A line open to other shippers would instead position Fujairah as a regional route around Hormuz, extending the UAE’s reach beyond its own production.

That would fit the direction the UAE has taken since leaving OPEC in May, with plans to invest in pipelines, rail, roads and at least three eastern ports to reduce its reliance on the strait. Neighbours are moving the same way: Saudi Arabia plans to expand its East-West pipeline, and Kuwait is in talks with both countries about alternative routes.

The backdrop explains the urgency. Hormuz was almost shut at the height of the Iran war, and while traffic has picked up, ships are still frequently targeted. Bypass routes are not immune either. Fujairah has been attacked several times during the conflict, and Saudi Arabia’s East-West line was briefly halted after an attack in September.

With ADNOC rejecting the report, the plan remains unconfirmed. The more concrete milestone for oil markets is the second pipeline, which ADNOC has told some Asian refiners could supply cargoes at Fujairah from early 2027. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.
